We show that there is an hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties of sets in a closed symplectic manifold: some sets cannot be displaced by symplectomorphisms from more sets than the others. We also find new examples of rigidity of intersections involving, in particular, specific fibers of moment maps of Hamiltonian torus actions, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds (following the works of P.Albers and P.Biran-O.Cornea), as well as certain, possibly singular, sets defined in terms of Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions. In addition, we get some geometric obstructions to semi-simplicity of the quantum homology of symplectic manifolds. The proofs are based on the Floer-theoretical machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states.

# Intersection Rigidity in Closed Symplectic Manifolds

This paper demonstrates that the subsets of a closed symplectic manifold are organized into a hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties. Within this hierarchy, certain sets exhibit a pronounced resistance to being displaced by symplectomorphisms, meaning that they cannot be moved off themselves—or off other prescribed sets—by the natural symmetries of the symplectic structure. Different classes of sets resist such displacement to varying degrees, and it is precisely this gradation that gives rise to the hierarchical structure that we make explicit.

Building on this framework, we identify several new examples of sets possessing intersection rigidity. Among these are specific fibers of the moment maps associated with Hamiltonian torus actions, whose distinguished position within the manifold accounts for their rigidity. We also establish intersection rigidity for a broad class of monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, thereby placing these fundamental objects of symplectic topology squarely within our hierarchy.

The scope of our results extends beyond smooth submanifolds. In particular, we show that certain sets which may be singular—defined in terms of Poisson-commutative subalgebras of the algebra of smooth functions on the manifold—also exhibit these rigidity properties. This perspective, formulated in algebraic terms via commuting Hamiltonians, allows us to capture rigidity phenomena for objects that lie outside the reach of purely geometric constructions.

These rigidity results carry significant algebraic consequences. Specifically, they yield geometric obstructions to the semi-simplicity of the quantum homology of symplectic manifolds. In this way, the intersection-theoretic behavior of subsets is linked to the structural properties of the quantum homology ring, providing a concrete bridge between geometric phenomena and algebraic invariants.

Our proofs rest on the Floer-theoretical machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states. These functionals, arising from spectral invariants in Floer and quantum homology, provide the analytical tools needed to detect and quantify intersection rigidity, and they underlie each of the results described above.

# Intersection Rigidity in Symplectic Manifolds via Partial Symplectic Quasi-States

## Abstract

This paper investigates the hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties of sets in closed symplectic manifolds using the Floer-theoretical machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states, examining which sets resist displacement by symplectomorphisms. The study reveals new examples of intersection rigidity—involving moment map fibers, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, and Poisson-commutative subalgebras—while also establishing geometric obstructions to the semi-simplicity of quantum homology, advancing the understanding of symplectic topology.

## 1. Introduction

One of the central themes in modern symplectic topology concerns the rigidity phenomena that distinguish symplectic geometry from its softer, purely topological counterpart. Whereas volume-preserving diffeomorphisms enjoy enormous flexibility, symplectomorphisms are constrained by subtle obstructions that first came to prominence with Gromov's non-squeezing theorem. Among these phenomena, *intersection rigidity* occupies a distinguished position: it asks whether a given subset of a symplectic manifold can be displaced from itself, or from other prescribed subsets, by the action of a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism or a more general symplectomorphism.

A subset $X$ of a closed symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$ is called *non-displaceable* if for every Hamiltonian diffeomorphism $\phi$, the intersection $\phi(X) \cap X$ is nonempty. More refined notions—such as stable non-displaceability, superheaviness, and heaviness—organize these rigidity properties into a hierarchy, each level encoding successively stronger constraints on how a set interacts with the symplectic structure. Understanding this hierarchy, and populating it with concrete examples, is the principal aim of the present work.

## 2. The Machinery of Partial Symplectic Quasi-States

The technical engine driving our investigation is the theory of *partial symplectic quasi-states*, functionals on the space of smooth observables that arise from the spectral invariants of Floer homology. These quasi-states, constructed from the deep structure of the quantum and Floer homology of $(M, \omega)$, provide a powerful and flexible criterion for detecting rigidity.

Concretely, a partial symplectic quasi-state $\zeta$ assigns to each smooth function a real number in a manner that is monotone, normalized, and partially additive—specifically additive on Poisson-commuting functions whose associated subalgebra is compatible with the spectral structure. A subset $X$ is *heavy* (respectively *superheavy*) with respect to $\zeta$ when the quasi-state values of functions supported on or vanishing near $X$ satisfy certain inequalities. The crucial point is that superheavy sets cannot be displaced from heavy sets, translating the algebraic properties of $\zeta$ into geometric statements about non-displaceability.

By systematically analyzing the interplay between these quasi-states and the underlying Floer theory, we obtain a unified framework in which diverse rigidity results can be derived and compared within a single hierarchy.

## 3. New Examples of Intersection Rigidity

### 3.1 Moment Map Fibers

Our first family of results concerns the fibers of moment maps associated with Hamiltonian torus actions. For a closed symplectic manifold equipped with such an action, the fibers of the moment map foliate the manifold, and a natural question is which of these fibers are non-displaceable. Building on and extending earlier work relating superheaviness to the vanishing of certain spectral obstructions, we identify new non-displaceable fibers by computing the relevant quasi-state values. In particular, we exhibit configurations in which fibers previously not known to be rigid are shown to be superheavy, thereby detecting a richer landscape of intersection rigidity than was accessible by prior methods.

### 3.2 Monotone Lagrangian Submanifolds

Lagrangian submanifolds constitute the most classical objects in symplectic intersection theory. We turn our attention to *monotone* Lagrangians—those for which the symplectic area and Maslov index of disks are positively proportional—and establish rigidity results by leveraging the Floer homology of these submanifolds. When the Lagrangian Floer homology is nonvanishing, the corresponding Lagrangian participates in the hierarchy as a heavy or superheavy set, and we derive new non-displaceability statements accordingly. These results illuminate the delicate relationship between the enumerative geometry of holomorphic disks and the coarse rigidity of the Lagrangian.

### 3.3 Poisson-Commutative Subalgebras

Finally, we consider *Poisson-commutative subalgebras* of the algebra of smooth functions—collections of observables that pairwise Poisson-commute, generalizing the classical notion of integrable systems. The additivity properties of partial symplectic quasi-states are especially well suited to this setting, and we use them to detect non-displaceable fibers of the associated integrable-type structures. This yields intersection rigidity phenomena for a broad class of commutative systems, extending the scope of classical results on integrable systems into a more general algebraic framework.

## 4. Obstructions to Semi-Simplicity of Quantum Homology

A striking outcome of our analysis is the discovery of *geometric obstructions to the semi-simplicity of quantum homology*. The quantum homology ring of a symplectic manifold, endowed with the quantum product deformed by counts of pseudoholomorphic spheres, may or may not decompose as a direct sum of fields—a property known as semi-simplicity. Semi-simplicity has profound consequences, as it guarantees the existence of a full complement of partial quasi-states and thereby strengthens the available rigidity conclusions.

We show, conversely, that certain geometric configurations of non-displaceable sets are incompatible with semi-simplicity. That is, the existence of particular rigidity phenomena imposes constraints that preclude the quantum homology from being semi-simple. This establishes a two-way dialogue between the algebraic structure of quantum homology and the geometric phenomenon of intersection rigidity: not only does algebraic structure yield rigidity, but rigidity in turn constrains algebraic structure.

## 5. Conclusion

By deploying the machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states, this paper advances the understanding of intersection rigidity across a spectrum of settings—moment map fibers, monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, and Poisson-commutative subalgebras—while simultaneously uncovering geometric obstructions to the semi-simplicity of quantum homology. Together, these results deepen the hierarchy of rigidity properties in closed symplectic manifolds and reinforce the intimate connection between Floer-theoretic algebra and symplectic geometry. We anticipate that the framework developed here will prove fruitful in future investigations of rigidity, integrable systems, and the fine structure of quantum homology.

# Hamiltonian, Lagrangian, and the Work of Peter Albers

## Two Faces of Classical Mechanics

The **Lagrangian** and **Hamiltonian** formulations represent two elegant and complementary ways of describing physical systems. Both go beyond Newton's original equations, offering deeper insight into the structure of dynamics and revealing symmetries that are otherwise hidden.

The **Lagrangian** formulation, developed by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, is built around a single function—the Lagrangian *L = T − V*, the difference between kinetic and potential energy. The trajectory a system actually follows is the one that makes the *action* stationary, a principle known as the principle of least action. From this variational idea, the Euler–Lagrange equations emerge, describing motion in terms of generalized coordinates and their velocities.

The **Hamiltonian** formulation, introduced by William Rowan Hamilton, reformulates mechanics in terms of positions and momenta rather than positions and velocities. The Hamiltonian function *H*, often equal to the total energy of the system, generates the evolution of the system through Hamilton's equations. This description lives naturally on *phase space* and carries a rich geometric structure known as symplectic geometry.

## The Bridge Between Them

The two formulations are connected by the **Legendre transformation**, which converts velocities into momenta and translates the Lagrangian into the Hamiltonian. Far from being redundant, each viewpoint has its strengths: the Lagrangian excels at handling constraints and symmetries, while the Hamiltonian provides the foundation for statistical mechanics, quantum theory, and the modern geometry of dynamics.

## Peter Albers and Modern Symplectic Geometry

In contemporary mathematics, these classical ideas continue to inspire deep research. **Peter Albers**, a mathematician working in symplectic and contact topology, has made significant contributions to the study of Hamiltonian dynamics and **Lagrangian** submanifolds. His work engages with tools such as Floer homology and Rabinowitz Floer homology, which probe the existence of periodic orbits and the intricate structure of energy surfaces in Hamiltonian systems.

By studying Lagrangian submanifolds—geometric objects that encode crucial information about a system—Albers and his collaborators have helped illuminate questions about rigidity, intersection phenomena, and the global behavior of Hamiltonian flows. This research shows how the classical language of Hamiltonians and Lagrangians, once a tool for describing planetary motion, now sits at the frontier of pure mathematics.

## Conclusion

From Lagrange's variational principle to Hamilton's phase-space dynamics, and onward to the modern symplectic geometry advanced by researchers like Peter Albers, these concepts form a continuous thread connecting physics and mathematics. Together they demonstrate how a few powerful ideas can shape our understanding of motion across centuries of scientific thought.

We show that the partial quasi-state formalism provides a robust computational tool: superheaviness of a subset guarantees that it intersects every set that is heavy with respect to the same quasi-state, thereby producing new classes of non-displaceable configurations that lie beyond the reach of classical Floer-theoretic methods. As applications, we exhibit explicit examples in toric symplectic manifolds, coadjoint orbits, and products, including families of Lagrangian tori and fibers of moment maps whose intersection rigidity we establish quantitatively. Our results unify and extend several known rigidity theorems, and they suggest that partial symplectic quasi-states encode subtle intersection-theoretic information not visible at the level of homology or classical symplectic capacities. We investigate the interplay between Hamiltonian torus actions and the quantum-theoretic invariants of closed symplectic manifolds, establishing new structural results in Floer theory and quantum homology. Let $(M, \omega)$ be a closed symplectic manifold equipped with a Hamiltonian action of a torus $T = (S^1)^k$ with moment map $\mu \colon M \to \mathfrak{t}^*$. We show that the equivariant Floer homology of the associated action, when localized at the fixed-point set $M^T$, admits a natural module structure over the small quantum homology ring $QH_*(M; \Lambda)$, and we compute the resulting spectral invariants in terms of the combinatorial data of the moment polytope.

Our main theorem asserts that when the fixed points are isolated, the quantum product is governed by a deformation of the classical Kirwan map, whose structure constants are counts of $J$-holomorphic spheres constrained by the Hamiltonian flow. As an application, we prove that the Seidel representation of $\pi_1(\mathrm{Ham}(M, \omega))$ factors through the toric part of the fundamental group of the automorphism group whenever $M$ is monotone and toric, refining earlier results of McDuff–Tolman. This yields explicit lower bounds for the Hofer–Zehnder capacity and confirms a form of the Chekanov–Hofer conjecture for a broad class of Fano toric varieties.

A key technical ingredient is a localization formula for the pair-of-pants product in the equivariant setting, obtained by analyzing the boundary strata of moduli spaces of Floer trajectories that break along gradient flow lines of $\mu$. We further exploit the resulting long exact sequences to detect obstructions to the existence of periodic orbits, showing that the presence of a Hamiltonian $T$-action forces the quantum homology to be semisimple after tensoring with the Novikov field. Combined with a filtration argument, this establishes the nondegeneracy of the Poincaré duality pairing on the Floer homology of the action and implies uniform bounds on the number of fixed points via a Morse–Bott spectral sequence.

Finally, we illustrate the theory with computations for products of projective spaces, coadjoint orbits, and Hirzebruch surfaces, where the module structure and Seidel elements are made fully explicit. Our results suggest a general dictionary between the convex geometry of moment polytopes and the multiplicative structure of quantum homology, and we conclude with conjectures relating the semisimplicity of $QH_*(M)$ to the existence of maximal Hamiltonian torus actions.

We introduce and systematically study a hierarchy of rigidity properties for compact subsets of symplectic manifolds, organized according to the strength of their resistance to displacement under Hamiltonian and symplectic isotopies. At the base of this hierarchy lie *non-displaceable* sets, which cannot be separated from themselves by any Hamiltonian diffeomorphism; ascending through *stably non-displaceable* sets (non-displaceable under stabilization by products with symplectic manifolds) and *superheavy* sets in the sense of Entov–Polterovich, we culminate in a notion of *totally rigid* sets, which resist displacement by the full symplectomorphism group. The central technical apparatus combines quantitative invariants derived from Floer homology and spectral numbers with quasimorphisms on the universal cover of the Hamiltonian group. We show that each rigidity class admits a characterization in terms of the vanishing or non-vanishing of associated symplectic quasi-states, providing a unified functional-analytic perspective on the hierarchy. As applications, we prove new non-displaceability results for fibers of moment maps in toric and non-toric settings, and we establish stability of the higher rigidity classes under symplectic reduction and fiber bundle constructions. We further relate our hierarchy to the coarse geometry of the group of symplectomorphisms, showing that ascent in the rigidity hierarchy corresponds to progressively stronger constraints on the Hofer and commutator length geometry of displacing paths.

Finally, we discuss obstructions to further refinement of the hierarchy and pose several questions concerning its behavior under symplectic capacities and its interaction with Lagrangian intersection phenomena.
